name: Kodimoottil Sri Bhadrakaali Temple
significance: A Bhadrakali shrine at Parippally in Kollam district with subsidiary shrines to Shiva, Ganapati and the Navagrahas. Its ten-day March mahotsavam, opened with pongala and closing with the Gajamela elephant procession, draws participants from every community.

name: Chandrasekhara Mahadeva Temple
significance: A nineteenth-century Shiva temple in Patia village on the northern edge of Bhubaneswar, enshrining a lingam set in a circular yoni pitha. Built of laterite and ashlar in the Kalinga idiom, it retains its vimana with a later concrete hall serving as jagamohana.

name: Astasambhu Siva Temples
significance: A group of eight tenth-century Shiva shrines in Bhubaneswar's old town, five of them aligned in a row locally called the Panchu Pandava. Built as small rekha deuls of grey sandstone in dry masonry, they stand between the Godavari and Bindusagar tanks.

name: Khidkaleshwar Mandir
significance: A Shiva temple on the bank of Khidkali Lake near Dombivli in Thane district, whose present structure was probably rebuilt in the seventeenth century. The complex also holds images of Ganesha and Hanuman, with smaller Dattatreya and Hanuman shrines nearby.
story: Local tradition holds that the Pandavas raised the shrine during their forest exile, when Yudhishthira wished to worship Shiva at the spot.

name: Beejamandal
significance: An unfinished and largely ruined temple at Jatkara near Khajuraho, first raised in the eighth century and rebuilt in the later eleventh. At about 34.6 m long its plinth exceeds the Kandariya Mahadeva, making it the largest temple footprint recorded at the site.

name: Badri Narayanan Temple
significance: A Vishnu temple at the entrance to Alagar Koil in Madurai district, where the principal image shows the god seated in meditation flanked by Nara and Narayana. It is modelled on the Badrinath temple of Uttarakhand and keeps daily rituals with monthly devotional singing.
story: By legend Kallalagar halts here on the eve of the Chittirai festival as he travels from Alagar Koil, and so misses his sister's wedding at Vandiyur.

name: Kodikkunnu Bhagavathy Temple
significance: An old Bhagavathy temple at Pallippuram near Pattambi in Palakkad district, where the goddess Bhadrakali is worshipped simply as Amma and shares the shrine with Shiva. It is unusual in opening three sacred entrances, to the north, east and west.
story: Temple tradition traces the goddess to Muthassiar Kavu Bhagavathi and her daughters, one of whom stayed on as the guardian deity of the kanakkan community.

name: Koorainadu Punukeeswarar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the Koranad neighbourhood of Mayiladuthurai, Tamil Nadu, where the god is worshipped as Punukeeswarar with the goddess Santhanayaki. The name preserves the civet-musk (punugu) association that gives the shrine its identity.
story: A civet is said to have found a lingam in a paddy field at Koranad and anointed it with its own fragrant musk, until Shiva appeared and granted the animal a place at Kailash.

name: Sri Chirakkakavu Bhagavathi Temple
builtDisplay: c. 13th c. (said to be 800 years old)
significance: A goddess temple at Thalassery in North Malabar where Kali is worshipped in three aspects as Thrigunaathmika. The structure is held to be at least eight centuries old and its foundation is credited to the Chirakkal raja of the Kolathiri line.
story: The goddess is said to have revealed herself at Vamal with her retinue, in a palace where the river meets the sea, and in the form of a divine fish.

name: Egowri Amman Temple, Vallam
significance: A goddess temple at Vallam, about 12 km from Thanjavur, whose earliest inscription belongs to the fortieth regnal year of the Chola king Parantaka I. Its image of Ambika is two-faced, one countenance fierce and the other serene, and the maha mandapa was added by Sevappa Nayak and Achuthappa Nayak in 1535.
story: The goddess Gowri is said to have ended the tyranny of the asura Thanjasuran by beheading him in his ox form.

name: Parassala Mahadeva Temple
significance: A centuries-old Shiva temple at Parassala near the Kerala-Tamil Nadu border, founded by Mallen Chembakaraman Delava of the Venad royal house and built largely in stone. Its Shiva faces west, a rare orientation in Kerala, and its rites have long admitted worshippers of every community.

name: Sree Maheswara Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Koorkenchery in Thrissur consecrated by the social reformer Narayana Guru in Malayalam Era 1092, with sub-shrines to Parvati, Ganapati, Murugan, Ayyappan, Krishna, Muthappan, Bhadrakali, the Navagrahas and the nagas. Its seven-day Thaipooya Mahotsavam is among the largest festivals around Thrissur after the Pooram.

name: Ahalya Sthan
significance: A temple at Kamtaul in Darbhanga district dedicated to Ahalya, wife of the sage Gautama, built between 1662 and 1682 under Maharaja Chhatra Singh and Maharaja Rudra Singh. It is described as the earliest Ram-Janaki temple in India.
story: The spot is remembered as the place where Ahalya, turned to stone by a curse after Indra's deception, rose again in her own body when Rama came there with Lakshmana and Vishvamitra.

name: Nallur Sundara Varadharaja Perumal Temple
builtDisplay: c. 16th c. (said to be 500 years old)
significance: A Vaishnava temple about five centuries old at Nallur in Tiruvannamalai district, where Vishnu is worshipped as Sundara Varadharaja Perumal with the goddess Sundaravalli Thayar. Garuda stands in worship at the feet of the main image, and Vaikuntha Ekadashi is the chief observance.

name: Kapilesvara Siva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the south-western edge of Kapilesvara village in old Bhubaneswar, built in the fourteenth century under the Gajapati ruler Kapilendra Deva on a site thought to hold an older shrine. The sanctum enshrines a lingam set in a circular yoni pitha.
story: Local legend calls this the birthplace of Shiva, honoured here as the father of the universe.

name: Sree Maha Ganapathy Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple at Thamarakulam in southern Kerala where Vigneshwara is regarded as the guardian of the whole locality, with further shrines to Dharmasastha, Murugan and Amman. Its principal observance is the Mandala Puja held as Sasthapreethi Samaradhana.

name: Sri Anjaneya Swamy Temple, Shamanur
significance: The village deity's shrine at Shamanur near Davangere, where a roughly six-foot Hanuman image is said to have been installed by Vyasaraja and the site traced back some eight centuries. The old temple was replaced by a Dravidian-style structure inaugurated in March 2000, and a three-day car festival follows ten days after Mahashivaratri.

name: Adisvaraswamy Jain Temple, Thanjavur
builtDisplay: c. 15th c. (said to be 600 years old)
significance: A Jain temple at Karanthattankudi near Thanjavur enshrining the first Tirthankara Rishabhanatha as Adisvaraswamy, with a two-tiered vimana, rajagopura and a sequence of mandapas added about three centuries ago. It is the only temple in Tamil Nadu with a separate shrine for the Jinavani.

name: Kumbakonam Brahma Temple
significance: A Kumbakonam temple whose moolavar is Vishnu as Vedanarayana Perumal, but which is best known for its shrine to Brahma alongside Saraswati, Gayatri and Yoganarasimha. Dedicated Brahma shrines are rare in India, the other well-known one being at Pushkar in Rajasthan.

name: Gondeshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Sinnar in Nashik district built under the Seuna (Yadava) dynasty, laid out as a panchayatana with the main shrine ringed by four subsidiary shrines to Surya, Vishnu, Parvati and Ganesha. One of the finest surviving Bhumija-style complexes in Maharashtra, it is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.
story: Local tradition credits its building to Rav Govinda, son of the Gavali chief Rav Singhuni, at a cost of two hundred thousand rupees.

name: Dubba Rajeswara Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Pembatla in Sarangapur mandal, Jagtial district, counted among the oldest and best-known shrines of the old Karimnagar region. Maha Shivaratri is its principal festival, when special buses run from Jagtial to the temple.

name: Kalahasteeswarar Temple, Kumbakonam
significance: A Shiva temple in Kumbakonam where the god is worshipped as Kalahasteeswarar with the goddess Gnanambikai, renovated by Serfoji of Thanjavur. It is one of the twelve Shiva temples tied to the Mahamaham festival held at Kumbakonam once every twelve years, and was reconsecrated in October 2015.

name: Arulmigu Koniamman Temple
significance: The guardian-deity temple of Coimbatore, on the north bank of the Noyyal, built in the eleventh century by descendants of the chieftain Kovan. Its 84-foot gopuram, finished in 2011, is the tallest in the region, and with Perur Pateeswarar it forms the city's pair of historic temples.
story: The city's name is said to descend from Koyamma, the goddess worshipped by the chieftain Kovan, whose name became Koniamma and gave Koyampuththoor its title.

name: Sree Balakrishna Swami Temple, Kuzhuppilly
significance: A Krishna temple in Kuzhuppilly village on Vypeen Island, maintained by the Goud Saraswat Brahmin community, whose idol was consecrated in 1895 and whose present building was completed in 1964. Its interior walls carry an extensive painted Dashavatara cycle, and sub-shrines honour Hanuman, Garuda, Ganapati, Lakshmi, the Navagrahas and Nagaraja.

name: Sree Bhuvaneswary Temple, Valamchuzhy
significance: One of the oldest temples in Pathanamthitta district, standing where the Achankovil river loops around the site on three sides. It is known for the Rudrapongala of the month of Kumbham and for a Padayani custom in which newborn children are presented to the goddess.
story: A devotee is said to have carried a flower from the Kodungallur Bhagavathy temple in which the goddess Bhuvaneswari dwelt, and was inspired to install her at Valamchuzhy.

name: Jalakandeswarar Temple, Vellore
significance: A Shiva temple inside Vellore Fort at the centre of the city, raised in 1550 by the Vijayanagara chieftain Chinna Bommi Reddi during the reign of Sadasiva Raya. It is noted for a nine-tier gopuram, richly carved stone pillars, monolithic sculpture and heavy wooden gates.
story: The lingam is said to have stood self-manifested within a great anthill ringed by standing water, which gave the god his name from jalam, water.

name: Kal Bhairav Temple, Ujjain
significance: The temple of Ujjain's guardian deity Kal Bhairav, on the bank of the Shipra, standing on older remains that yielded Paramara-period images of Shiva, Parvati, Vishnu and Ganesha. The present Maratha-style building with its deepmalika lamp tower is credited to a restoration by Mahadaji Shinde after 1761, and liquor is still offered to the deity as one of the five tantric panchamakara offerings.

name: Kaliyuga Varadaraja Perumal Temple, Kallankurichi
significance: A Vaishnava temple about 10 km from Ariyalur where the object of worship is a pillar rather than an anthropomorphic image. The building is roughly five centuries old and shows Vijayanagara-period Dravidian work, with sculpted pillars filling the ardha mandapa.
story: A cowherd named Maangan is said to have gone looking for a missing pregnant cow, found her newly calved at the spot, and so learned of a wooden pillar of Vishnu there that held great power.

name: Sreenarayanapuram Mahavishnu Temple
significance: An eighteenth-century Vishnu temple at Manakala, about 4 km from Adoor in Pathanamthitta district. It is one of the few Kerala Vishnu temples that keeps the ten-day Dasavatarachartu festival, in which one avatar of Vishnu is worshipped on each day.

name: Lakshmi Narasimha Temple, Antarvedi
significance: A Narasimha temple at Antarvedi in Konaseema district, standing where the Vasishta Godavari meets the Bay of Bengal, with Lakshmi worshipped here as Rajyalakshmi. Begun in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries and recorded as completed in Shalivahana Saka 1745 (1823 CE), its building by Kopanathi Krishnamma is attested by a stone inscription at the site.

name: Masani Amman Temple
significance: A Shakta temple at Anaimalai near Pollachi, in existence before 1000 CE and kept by many families as their kuladevi shrine. Its goddess is unusual in being shown reclining, some 15 feet from head to foot, holding a damaru, a fire bowl, a kumkum bowl and a trident.
story: Local tradition tells of a woman executed for eating from a cruel king's mango grove, whose execution stone came to be worshipped with offerings of ground red chilli.

name: Rajendracholiswarar Temple, Ilaiyankudi
significance: A Shiva temple at Ilaiyankudi in Ramanathapuram district, counted among the Vaippu Sthalams praised in Tamil Saiva devotional verse, with Gnanambikai as the goddess. It is revered as the birthplace of the Nayanar saint Ilayankudi Maranar, and keeps Maha Shivaratri, Kanda Sashti and Karthikai.

name: Sree Venu Gopala Swamy Temple, Purakkad
builtDisplay: c. 17th c. (said to be 400 years old)
significance: One of the oldest Gowda Saraswat Brahmin temples anywhere, raised at Purakkad in Alappuzha district about four hundred years ago by families who left Goa under Portuguese pressure to convert and were granted land by the Raja of Chembakassery. The temple rises about 29 m and keeps Krishna Janmashtami, Kartika Purnima and Navaratri.

name: Seetha Devi Temple
significance: A temple at Pulpally in Wayanad established in the eighteenth century by Pazhassi Raja, who long managed it, and one of very few in Kerala where Sita's sons Lava and Kusha receive worship. Its tank is among the largest in Wayanad and the annual festival falls in the first week of January.
story: It is told that after Rama abandoned her, Sita came to Pulpally and was sheltered by the sage Valmiki, whose ashram is remembered nearby.

name: Someswarar Temple, Kumbakonam
significance: A Shiva temple at Kumbakonam where the god is worshipped as Someswarar with the goddess Somasundari, its present masonry raised by the Nayaks in the sixteenth century behind a five-tier rajagopuram. The shrine is a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung by the Nayanars in the seventh-century Tevaram.
story: The name is explained by Chandra, the moon, having worshipped Shiva here, and the lingam is held to be swayambhu, self-formed.

name: Somesvara Siva Temple
significance: A living Shiva temple within the Kharakhia Baidyanath precinct in old Bhubaneswar, dated on architectural grounds to the tenth or eleventh century. It pairs a rekha deul vimana with a pidha deul jagamohana and enshrines a lingam in a circular yonipitha, with Shivaratri, Sankranti and Mahavishuva Sankranti observed.

name: Veeramakaliamman Temple, Arantangi
significance: A goddess temple about 2 km from Arantangi in Pudukkottai district, where Veeramakaliamman is enshrined seated, with a vasantha mandapa and maha mandapa and shrines of Vinayaka and Karuppar in front. Four daily pujas are performed and festivals run through the Tamil year.
story: The place, then called Veeravanam, is said to have been visited by the Pandavas during their forest exile, who worshipped the goddess here.

name: Jambukaranyesvarar Temple, Kundalur
significance: A Shiva temple at Kundalur in Tiruvarur district, some 20 km from Kumbakonam, with the lingam worshipped as Jambukaranyesvarar and the goddess as Anandavalli. It is one of the Vaippu Sthalams named in the hymns of the Nayanar Appar.
story: The place is remembered as Jambu Karanyam, where Sita is said to have worshipped and the sage Roma Maharishi performed penance.

name: Sree Shivashakthi Mahaganapathi Temple
significance: A temple at Keezhammakam in Chenkal panchayat, southern Thiruvananthapuram district, holding Shiva, Parvati and Ganapati together. Ganesh Chaturthi is its chief festival, with further observances from Chithra Pournami and at Maha Shivaratri.

name: Sri Laxmi Venkatesh Temple
significance: A Goud Saraswat Brahmin temple at Kanhangad in Kasaragod district, affiliated to the Kashi Math, whose consecration rites began in 1864 and concluded on Akshaya Tritiya in 1865. It was founded at the instance of Srimad Bhuvanendra Tirtha with the support of the four Chowguli families.
story: The image is said to have come from Innoli, whose community could not sustain the offerings, and the swami is remembered as asking the god to accept whatever naivedya the people of Kanhangad could give and to return four times the blessing.

name: Sri Lakshmi Narasimha Temple, Thalassery
significance: A Goud Saraswat Brahmin temple of the Dvaita tradition at Thalassery, built in 1831 on the site of an older shrine after the merchant Devdas Bhandari gave the Lakshmi Narasimha image early in the nineteenth century. It also holds Kodanda Rama and Venkataramana, has a three-tiered simhasana, and unusually faces north; it was consecrated by Sumatheendra Tirtha, fifteenth pontiff of the Kashi Math.

name: Sree Venugopala Krishna Swami Devasthan
significance: A Krishna temple at Chendamangalam in Ernakulam district, founded by settled Goud Saraswat Brahmin families under Chennoth Parambil Dasa Prabhu on land given by the Paliath Valiyachan of the Paliyam house, with the pratishta performed on 30 April 1900. It keeps a stone principal image with a separate utsava murti and figures of Garuda and Hanuman, and its six-day festival falls in Vaisakha.

name: Andalurkavu
significance: A very old kavu near Dharmadam by Thalassery in Kannur district, where Rama is worshipped as Daivathaar with Lakshmana as Angakkaran and Hanuman as Bappuran, and which is closely tied to the Thiyya community. A small bow and arrow is offered in the name of every Thiyya boy born in the four surrounding regions, giving it the byname Andalure Aayiram Ville, the thousand bows of Andalur.
